active_paradigms.idea: True greedy LPT assignment to GPUs with a vectorized heap-free argmin loop, replacing the serpentine heuristic
active_paradigms.description: The current balanced_packing uses a fixed serpentine deal pattern, which is only an approximation of least-loaded greedy. Replace Step 3 (packing physical experts to GPUs) with a true greedy: sort physical experts by load descending per layer, then iteratively assign each expert to the GPU with the currently minimum total load. This can be done with a small Python loop over items (num_replicas is small, e.g. 64-256), where per-iteration work is a vectorized argmin over the num_gpus load vector plus an index_add update — O(n log n) sort plus O(n*m) assignment with tiny constants. Since the loop is over experts (not layers), all layers can be batched: maintain a [num_layers, num_gpus] cumulative load tensor and for each sorted position take argmin along dim=-1. This guarantees each GPU gets exactly phy_experts_per_gpu by tracking counts and forbidding full GPUs (mask them with +inf). Greedy LPT has a 4/3 approximation guarantee for makespan, strictly better than serpentine on skewed loads.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Load balance quality (max GPU load / mean) — the primary balance metric in the evaluator; also reduces variance across GPUs.
active_paradigms.cautions: Must enforce exact expert counts per GPU (mask full GPUs). Keep per-layer independence: layers are batched so no cross-layer loop needed. The Python loop length equals experts-per-node, not layers, so runtime stays well within timeout. Tie-break argmin deterministically (lowest index) for reproducibility.

active_paradigms.idea: Proportional (water-filling) replication instead of max-first greedy in replicate_experts
active_paradigms.description: The current replicate_experts greedily gives each redundant expert to the logical expert with the highest load/count ratio. This over-replicates hot experts early and ignores how replication interacts with the subsequent GPU packing. Replace it with a proportional water-filling allocation: compute for each layer the load vector w, and allocate the num_redundant replicas so that the post-replication effective loads w_i / c_i are as equal as possible. Concretely, run a bisection on a threshold t: for a candidate t, the ideal replica count is c_i(t) = ceil(w_i / t), and find the smallest t such that sum(c_i) equals num_phy (binary search on t over [max(w)/num_phy, max(w)]). Then fix up rounding with a greedy pass to hit exactly num_phy replicas. This yields near-perfectly equalized effective expert loads, which makes the downstream packing trivially balanced.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Post-replication load uniformity (w_i/c_i spread), which directly bounds the achievable GPU balance — the dominant term in the score for skewed workloads.
active_paradigms.cautions: Bisection needs ~40-60 iterations of a vectorized ceil+sum over [layers, num_log], which is fast. Handle edge cases: experts with zero load get c_i=1; ensure c_i >= 1 always. The final fix-up must be deterministic. Keep the rank/logcnt bookkeeping identical to the existing interface.

active_paradigms.idea: Joint layer-aware assignment via scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment on a cost matrix of expert-to-GPU placements
active_paradigms.description: The hierarchical approach packs groups to nodes first, then experts to GPUs, and each stage is greedy — errors compound across stages. Instead, formulate the final expert-to-GPU assignment as a balanced assignment problem: build a cost matrix C[e][g] = load of expert e if placed on GPU g (with capacity constraints), and use scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment on an expanded matrix where each GPU is replicated phy_experts_per_gpu times (columns = num_replicas slots), so each expert replica occupies exactly one slot. Cost entries can encode node locality: add a penalty for placing an expert in a node different from its group's majority node, preserving the intra-node NVLink benefit that the hierarchical method provides. Because the assignment is optimal for the given cost, the GPU loads are minimized directly rather than through two greedy stages. Replication counts from water-filling (idea 2) feed in as duplicate rows for replicated experts.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Directly minimizes maximum/sum GPU load imbalance in one optimal step instead of two greedy stages; also controls node-locality penalty.
active_paradigms.cautions: linear_sum_assignment is O(n^3) on a num_replicas x num_replicas matrix (e.g., 256x256) per layer — run per layer, or stack layers as independent calls; keep total calls equal to num_layers (typically 10-60), well within timeout. Rows must be expert replicas (with duplicates for replicated experts), columns are physical slots. Convert the assignment result back into phy2log, rank, and logcnt tensors consistent with the expected output format. Use float64 costs for numerical stability.

tried_paradigms.idea: Replace the serpentine packing with a true vectorized LPT (Longest Processing Time) assignment using heap-like bucketed scatter, then refine with pairwise swap local search on GPU loads
tried_paradigms.description: The current balanced_packing is a fixed serpentine pattern that only approximates least-loaded assignment. Instead, compute per-pack running sums incrementally: after sorting weights descending, assign each item to the currently least-loaded pack by maintaining pack sums and using torch.scatter_add with a per-block argmin over pack loads. Since each pack must receive exactly n/m items, use a two-phase approach: first run greedy least-loaded assignment (vectorized across layers via a small loop over blocks of items, where within each block every pack gets exactly one item chosen by a linear_sum_assignment per block — but simpler: within each block, match the block's sorted items to packs via reversed-order assignment, which is provably optimal for a block). Then apply a bounded local-search refinement: repeatedly find the most-loaded and least-loaded GPU, and move one expert from the former to the latter if it reduces max load, limited to a fixed iteration budget (e.g., 50 sweeps) to keep runtime low. This directly attacks the max-GPU-load metric that dominates the balance score.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Load balance quality (max GPU load, variance across GPUs) while keeping runtime within budget
tried_paradigms.cautions: The per-block assignment must preserve the exact count constraint (n/m items per pack). Keep all operations on CPU tensors with torch single-threaded (evaluator forces 1 thread). Bound local search iterations so total runtime stays well under the timeout.
tried_paradigms.approach_type: torch.scatter_add + greedy LPT with bounded local search

tried_paradigms.idea: Replace the greedy replicate_experts loop with a water-filling / proportional replication allocation solved in closed form, then round with a largest-remainder method
tried_paradigms.description: The current replication loop greedily adds replicas one at a time to the expert with the highest load/replica-count ratio, which is O(num_redundant) sequential steps and also suboptimal (it ignores interactions with the subsequent packing step). Instead, compute the ideal continuous replica count for each logical expert via water-filling: find the level L such that sum over experts of max(1, w_e / L) equals num_phy, solvable with a few bisection iterations (fully vectorized, ~30 iterations of a vectorized comparison). Then round the fractional replica counts to integers using the largest-remainder method (Hamilton apportionment): give each expert floor(count), then distribute the remaining replicas to the largest fractional remainders, guaranteeing the total equals num_phy and every expert gets at least 1. This is O(log(precision)) vectorized passes instead of O(num_redundent) Python-loop iterations, improving both speed and balance quality. The resulting per-replica loads are exactly w_e / count_e, which the water-filling level makes near-uniform across all replicas.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Both runtime (removes the sequential Python loop) and balance (near-uniform per-replica loads before packing)
tried_paradigms.cautions: Bisection must handle the degenerate case where all weights are equal (any L works — pick the exact value). Ensure the largest-remainder rounding respects the minimum of 1 replica per expert and the exact total num_phy. Keep everything in float32/float64 torch tensors, no Python loops over experts.

tried_paradigms.idea: Joint two-level optimization: fix the node assignment via balanced_packing, then solve the within-node expert-to-GPU assignment with scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment on a cost matrix that penalizes both load imbalance and replica co-location
tried_paradigms.description: The current algorithm makes packing decisions greedily and independently at each level, ignoring the final objective. After computing per-node physical expert loads (w_e / count_e), construct a cost matrix C[i, g] for assigning physical expert i to GPU g within a node, where the cost encodes placing an expert on a GPU whose current accumulated load plus this expert's load exceeds the target average (use a convex quadratic penalty on deviation from target load per GPU). Solve the assignment with scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment per (layer, node) — with num_phy per node typically small (tens), this is fast (Hungarian is O(n^3) on small matrices, microseconds-to-milliseconds). Because the linear assignment can't capture the bin-packing interaction fully, iterate: solve assignment, update GPU loads, re-solve with updated penalties, for a small fixed number of rounds (e.g., 5). This replaces the heuristic serpentine packing at the GPU level with a near-optimal assignment given the penalty structure, while the top-level node packing stays cheap.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Primary balance score at the GPU level (the finest granularity and likely the dominant metric term)
tried_paradigms.cautions: linear_sum_assignment requires a square or rectangular cost matrix; pad with dummy zero-load experts if num_phy per node is not divisible by GPUs-per-node. Note the evaluator forces single-threaded execution — Hungarian on small matrices is fine but avoid calling it per-layer per-node if that exceeds a few thousand calls; batch identical structures where possible. The count constraint (experts per GPU must be exactly equal) must be enforced by padding the cost matrix to a square assignment problem.
